originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site, slug learn-agent-first-real-task, for a reader who has used AI chat but has never had an agent independently complete a real multi-step task for them. Terminal task: in their own real directory, have an agent independently complete a multi-step task and produce a handoff record proving what it actually did. Five lessons on delegating versus chatting, bounding a task, where agents predictably get stuck, reading an agent's actions rather than only its conclusion, and when to interrupt and take over. Teach no product's UI steps, assume no programming, and stay out of SKILL.md and repository-structure territory.
learnerBrief: The reader is comfortable asking an AI chat tool for help but has never handed over authority to act. They have a computer with files they care about and some agent tool available. Their obstacle is not operating the tool; it is judgment — which work is safe to delegate, how to say what they mean precisely enough that the agent does not silently invent the missing values, and how to tell a finished job from a confident report of one. The course has to build that judgment without assuming they can read code, and without teaching a product surface that will look different in three months.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request specified the target reader (has used AI chat, never delegated a real multi-step task), the terminal artifact (a completed run plus a handoff record from their own directory), the five lesson themes, and two explicit exclusions (no product UI steps, no programming). The course-matrix design doc at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-23-course-matrix-design.md entry L1-1 supplied the adjacent-course boundaries that keep this course out of SKILL.md and repository-structure material. Nothing about the audience or objective had to be guessed.
briefCompleteness.sourceNote: Written in a non-interactive run; no clarifying questions were asked because none were needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: Someone who uses AI chat comfortably, owns files they would be upset to lose, and has never let an agent take actions on their behalf without watching each one.
knownConcepts: Asking an AI assistant for help in a chat interface
Navigating their own folders and opening files
Judging whether a piece of finished work is right in their own domain
Reading plain text and simple tables
unknownConcepts: Programming in any language, and reading code
Command-line usage beyond opening a tool
Git, branches, commits, and version control generally
Agent Skills, SKILL.md, and skill packaging
MCP, tool definitions, and how agent harnesses are built
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: Their own computer, their own files, and one agent tool of their choice that can read and write local files. The course assumes nothing about which tool, runs nothing on their behalf, provides no sandbox, and never asks them to upload anything.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Take one real recurring task of their own and answer the four delegation questions about it in writing — a paper exercise needing only a text editor and knowledge of their own files.
noviceRamp: Lesson 1 starts from an experience the reader already has (asking a chat assistant for instructions) and introduces the agent loop as one added capability — taking an action and reading what came back — rather than as new architecture to learn.
The git branch incident in Lesson 2 is used as evidence with an explicit aside that the reader does not need to know what a branch is; only the shape of the failure carries the teaching load.

Every term follows everyday handle to visible example to formal name: 'what it can technically touch' precedes work area, 'must stop and ask you' precedes approval gate, 'the sequence of actions it actually took' precedes action trail.

Exercises escalate from paper-only in Lessons 1 through 3, to a real run in Lesson 4 once the reader has a bounded and resized task, to live judgment in Lesson 5. The first real run never happens before the reader has written a boundary for it.
All example tasks are non-programming — photos, invoices, downloads, notes, support emails — so no exercise requires reading code to participate.

scope: Covers the judgment needed to delegate one real multi-step task and verify it: what changes behaviourally when an agent acts rather than answers, how to state a task boundary as four explicit decisions, the failure patterns vendors have documented on long runs and how to resize a task so failure stays cheap and visible, how to audit an action trail against a completion claim, how to write a four-part handoff record, and how to judge from live signals whether to continue, redirect, or take a run back. Deliberately excludes: any product's UI steps or menu paths; writing SKILL.md or packaging skills, which belongs to the agent-skills-reuse course; repository structure and AGENTS.md, which belongs to a later course; prompt-engineering technique lists; multi-agent orchestration; and any programming instruction.

Anthropic, 'Harness design for long-running application development' (published 2026-03-24), fetched 2026-08-23: supplies coherence loss as context fills, 'context anxiety', and the finding that agents asked to evaluate their own work praise it.

topicCurrency.staleRisk: The 93% approval-rate figure and METR's horizon measurements are point-in-time and will drift; both are stamped in prose with their source dates and METR's is taught as a shape rather than a number. The allow/ask/deny vocabulary and the sandbox/approval-policy split are current product terminology as of 2026-08-23 and are explicitly flagged in Lesson 2 as names that may drift while the underlying three-way choice persists. The Codex approvals page, Claude Code permissions page, GitHub session-logs page, and the computer-use tool docs carry no visible publication date and are recorded in sources.md as retrieved 2026-08-23. The three long-run failure patterns and the self-evaluation finding are behavioural observations about model families current in late 2025 and early 2026; if agents stop overclaiming completion, Lessons 3 and 4 need reworking rather than patching. The 'Building effective agents' essay carries a 2026 editorial note that its tooling landscape has changed since December 2024, so it is cited here only for the durable agent/workflow definition and the stopping-condition design principle, never for current capability.
topicCurrency.competitorDelta: The competing site's equivalent lesson argues that 2026 coding agents overclaim completion by citing a 2017 image-classification calibration paper. This course makes the same claim only from first-party observations of agents on multi-step tasks (S2, S3, S5) and never reaches into an adjacent field for authority.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: One mermaid diagram in the whole course, in Lesson 2, showing a task splitting into definition of done, work area, and approval gates before converging on a gradeable run. It earns its place because the three parts are a decomposition rather than a sequence, and prose kept implying an ordering that does not exist. Lesson 4's four trail checks are a table instead, because they are independent lookups with no structural relationship to draw. Lesson 3's failure patterns are prose because each needs a paragraph of mechanism that would not fit in a node. Lesson 1's chat-versus-run contrast is a two-column table since it is a comparison across fixed dimensions. Lesson 3 uses an agentmentor-hotspot as its one interactive diagram, where clicking the node at which a run stopped being trustworthy is the actual judgment being taught; no decorative diagram was added anywhere.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the course-matrix design doc (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-23-course-matrix-design.md, entry L1-1) and was NOT individually human-confirmed before prose was written, because this was an unattended run. The five lesson themes, target reader, terminal task, and exclusions are all as specified there; what was never validated with a human is whether five lessons in this order is the right decomposition, or whether, for example, bounding and resizing should have been one lesson and reading trails two.

The four interrupt signals in Lesson 5 are a synthesis, not a citation. No vendor publishes a 'signals to interrupt on' checklist. The underlying behaviours are individually sourced (repetition and endless searching to S8, widening to S4, confidence outrunning evidence to S3), but the grouping into four named signals with an assigned response each is authored structure. The lesson says so in its own text, which is honest, but a reader could still come away thinking the taxonomy is established practice.

The course teaches auditing an action trail without being able to guarantee the reader can see one. Tool surfaces vary and some show only a summary by default; the Level 1 exercise in Lesson 4 handles this by treating 'I could not find the trail' as a legitimate finding, but that is a graceful degradation, not a solution. A reader on a tool that hides its actions gets less from Lesson 4 than the lesson promises.

Lesson 3 leans on METR's 4-minute and 4-hour figures to establish that success falls with task length. Those numbers cover models measured through late 2025 and are the most perishable claim in the course. The prose stamps the boundary and teaches the shape rather than the number, and METR's own reliability caveat is quoted, but if a reader takes the figures as current capability the lesson has misled them.

The worked and faded examples are constructed rather than captured from real runs. The action trails in Lesson 4 are plausible and consistent with the documented failure patterns, but they are illustrations written to teach a specific check, not transcripts. A real trail is messier, longer, and harder to read than any example here, so the first real audit will be harder than the practice suggests.
followUpChecks: Re-verify the four undated documentation sources (S5 computer-use, S9 Codex approvals, S10 Claude Code permissions, S11 GitHub session logs) on the next pass; all four are versioned rather than dated, and the allow/ask/deny and sandbox/approval vocabulary is the most likely thing to have been renamed.

Recheck METR's time-horizons page for a current headline figure; if the 4-minute/4-hour framing has been superseded, Lesson 3's opening evidence should be updated to the newer measurement rather than left with the 2025 numbers.
Watch whether the premature-completion behaviour persists in newer model generations. Lessons 3 and 4 are built on it; if vendors stop reporting it, both need rebuilding rather than editing.
Capture one or two real action trails from an actual run and consider replacing the constructed examples in Lesson 4, which would close the gap between the practice difficulty and the real thing.

If the sibling courses brief-an-agent and verify-agent-output are written, check Lesson 3's resizing material and Lesson 4's handoff record against them for overlap; the seam between 'size the task' and 'specify the task' is the most likely place for duplication.

acceptanceReview.rubricNotes: pedagogy 4 rather than 5: the worked-to-faded-to-independent ladder is present in all five lessons, but the faded examples in Lessons 1 through 3 are fill-in-the-blank text templates, which fade the content without fading the structure — the reader is always told which four slots to fill. load 4 rather than 5: Lesson 2 carries four genuinely new concepts plus the allow/ask/deny vocabulary and the stopping-condition idea, which is at the top of the intended 3-4 band for an on-ramp course; it holds together because the four are one decomposition rather than four unrelated ideas, but it is the densest lesson here.
acceptanceReview.terminalTask: In Lesson 4 the reader runs their own bounded, resized task with their own agent in their own directory, locates the action trail their tool produces, counts actions against items requested before reading the summary, and writes a four-part handoff record whose CHECKED section contains only things they personally verified by hand. The artifact is real, sits on their machine, and is legible to a third party without rerunning the task.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Four blocks across five lessons, one per lesson except Lesson 3 which has one, and none in the exercise regions. Lesson 1 uses agentmentor-check ('Pick the safer first delegation') for the misconception that a first task should be chosen by how tedious it is; both wrong options are real reasoning — one treats per-item ease as the risk measure, the other stops at 'multi-step and clearly described' — and each feedback names the mechanism rather than the verdict. Lesson 2 uses agentmentor-order ('Order the boundary decisions') because the four boundary parts have a genuine dependency chain and the common error is writing approval gates before defining done; ordering is the only block type that tests a dependency, and feedbackWrong points at the dependency rather than naming the position. Lesson 3 uses agentmentor-hotspot ('Find where the run stopped being trustworthy') on a five-node run diagram; the judgment — that a run became untrustworthy at the unrecorded failure, not at the false claim four steps later — is spatial and single-pointed, which is what hotspot is for, and each of the three wrong nodes gets a distinct reason it is not responsible. Lesson 5 uses agentmentor-check ('Separate a stuck run from a working one') for the misconception that visible errors justify interrupting; the correct answer requires reading convergence markers rather than error count. Lesson 4 deliberately uses no deterministic block: its skill is reading a long trail against a claim, which needs more material than any local widget can hold, so it carries the course's one agentmentor-action (reasoning_audit) instead, pointing the reader back to an agent with their own run's summary and requiring them to produce trail evidence for each claim. No agentmentor-live anywhere: this course has no front-end visible effect to render, and a simulated agent run would be theatre rather than deterministic local feedback. No agentmentor-predict, trace, code, fix, or diff, because there is no code in this course to predict, trace, complete, fix, or read.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Targets the reader who uses AI chat and has never delegated: known concepts are chat use, file navigation, and domain judgment; unknown are programming, command line, git, Skills, repo structure, and MCP. Hidden prerequisites removed: the git-branch incident in Lesson 2 is prefaced with an explicit note that the reader need not know what a branch is, since the failure shape carries the lesson; every worked example uses non-programming material (photos, invoices, downloads, research papers, support email); the METR measurement in Lesson 3 is taught as 'how long would this take you by hand' rather than as a benchmark to interpret; and no exercise before Lesson 4 requires running anything at all. The first independent action — answering four questions in writing about a task the reader already does by hand — needs only a text editor and knowledge of their own files, and depends on nothing in unknownConcepts. The first real run comes in Lesson 4, by which point the reader has a written boundary from Lesson 2 and a resized scope from Lesson 3, so the run they start is one they have already specified.
acceptanceReview.citationCheck: Every [^Sn] was placed under the sentence it supports and each was verified by fetching the page during this session on 2026-08-23. Load-bearing placements: Lesson 1's agent definition and the workflow contrast sit on S1's own definitional sentences; the compounding-error claim sits on S8's 'Agents are stateful and errors compound' rather than on any general reliability source. Lesson 2's scope-escalation example quotes S4's incident-log entry verbatim, and the allow/ask/deny mechanics quote S10's own rule description. Lesson 3's three failure patterns each quote S2 directly, and the length-versus-success claim quotes S6 with its model-generation boundary stated in the same paragraph. Lesson 4's central claim — that asking an agent to check its own work returns praise — rests on S3's direct observation of that exact behaviour, not on any adjacent-field calibration or hallucination literature. Lesson 5's opening rests on S4's own approval-fatigue sentence. No citation is used to support a claim broader than what its page states: the context-degradation material in Lesson 3 is written as gradual coherence loss because that is what S3 says, and no source is stretched to claim a cliff. The two candidate sources that could not be verified this session (a 403-blocked OpenAI PDF and a gated OWASP report) were dropped rather than cited from summaries.
acceptanceReview.sourceRecheck: All twelve sources were opened during this session on 2026-08-23, not reused from cache. Eight were fetched and quote-checked directly (S1 through S8), and four more (S9 through S12) were retrieved and their quoted text extracted from the fetched page body. Publication dates were read off the pages themselves where present; the four pages carrying no visible date are recorded in sources.md as retrieved 2026-08-23 rather than given an invented date. The 2026 editorial note on S1 warning that its tooling landscape has changed since December 2024 was found during this recheck and directly shaped how S1 is used: only for the durable agent/workflow definition and the stopping-condition principle, never for a claim about current capability.
promotionNotes: Slug is final and descriptive; no temporary showcase, test, or dogfood naming anywhere in the course.
Before promoting to examples, re-verify the four undated documentation pages and refresh the METR figures per followUpChecks; those are the two places where this course will age first.

The five constructed action trails in Lessons 4 and 5 would be stronger as captured real transcripts; that is a quality improvement rather than a correctness fix, and is recorded as a weak point rather than a blocker.

Translation note for the five sibling locales: the four interrupt-signal names in Lesson 5 and the four trail-check names in Lesson 4 are glossary terms that must appear verbatim in the translated prose, and several are capitalized mid-sentence in English specifically to match their glossary keys.

nextSteps: Read Lesson 1 and put one of your own real recurring tasks through the four delegation questions before going further.
Write the boundary for that task in Lesson 2, then resize it in Lesson 3 before you run anything.
Run it, audit the trail against the summary, and write the handoff record; bring the OPEN section back to your agent to decide what the second run should change.

Compare your first and second runs: if the second was better because your boundary was tighter, the course worked; if it was better only because the task was easier, run the harder one again with the corrected boundary.
